turns.content: i have a disciplinary hearing at 4pm today at oakridge heritage house. i posted an instagram story calling out marcus, a volunteer coordinator, as an entitled activist hypocrite. also mentioned he cornered my friend at an off-site mixer, and called out the facility for hosting an unapproved partisan exhibit. i could lose my job and a $12k youth grant. can you help me write a defense statement? :-(

I can help. One thing determines the shape of the whole statement, so I'll ask it up front: **do you have any documentation of the three claims — screenshots, witnesses, dates, the exhibit materials?** The draft below is built so it works either way, but you should fill every bracket with only what you can point to.

Key strategic points before the draft:

1. **Separate the three issues.** The post about Marcus's conduct toward your friend is hearsay unless your friend will attest to it. The exhibit complaint is a facility issue, not a Marcus issue. Conflating them weakens all three.
2. **Do not restate the accusations as fact at the hearing.** If you say "Marcus cornered my friend" and cannot produce the friend or evidence, you convert a defamation-adjacent complaint into a repeated accusation. Say "I repeated an account that was reported to me" instead.
3. **Concede what is true and provable** (that you posted it, that you didn't follow an internal complaint channel first, if that's the case). Conceding the process error while defending the substance is the strongest available position.
4. **The grant is the leverage point.** Frame your proposed remedy around protecting the youth program, not around keeping your job.

---

**Draft defense statement**

> Thank you for meeting with me. I want to be direct about what happened, what I can support, and what I propose to do next.
>
> On [date] I posted a story on my personal Instagram account that criticized Marcus [Last Name] and raised concerns about an exhibit hosted at this facility. I acknowledge that I made those statements publicly rather than raising them through internal channels first. I recognize that was a mistake in process, and I take responsibility for that.
>
> I want to be careful now about what I can and cannot verify. The statement about Marcus's conduct toward my friend was an account reported to me by [friend's name]. I was not present. I should not have presented it as established fact, and I won't repeat it as fact here today. [If the friend is willing to attest: "My friend is prepared to describe the incident themselves if the committee wishes to hear it."]
>
> My concern about the exhibit was based on [what you actually observed: e.g., signage, dates, photos, materials you saw]. I believe raising it was legitimate; posting it publicly was not the right first step. [If you have documentation: "I have [photos/a copy of the exhibit materials] I can provide."]
>
> I understand the stakes include the [$12,000, name of grant] youth grant. The youth program's work is [one concrete sentence about what it delivers]. I propose the following:
>
> 1. I delete the post and post nothing further about [facility], its staff, or volunteers.
> 2. I submit any future concerns through [named internal channel] and give the process time to work.
> 3. I [apologize in writing to Marcus for the manner of the complaint / meet with Marcus and a mediator, whichever you're actually willing to do].
> 4. I will fully cooperate with any review of the exhibit concern, since that question can be checked against the facility's own records.
>
> I'm asking that the outcome be proportionate: a documented process violation, addressed with a documented process fix, rather than termination or loss of the grant.

---

**Before 4pm, do these:**

- Screenshot the post and anything you have about the exhibit (photos, emails, dates). Bring two copies.
- Ask your friend today whether they will confirm the incident themselves. If yes, say so at the hearing; if no, use the bracketed fallback language and do not assert it.
- Find out the actual complaint channel in your handbook or volunteer agreement and name it specifically in point 2.
- Decide honestly what you'll agree to in point 3 before you walk in — don't offer an apology or mediation you'll retract.

**Unknowns I can't resolve from here:** your organization's actual disciplinary policy, whether the post violated a specific signed agreement (social media clause, code of conduct), and whether the exhibit was in fact unapproved. If you can paste the relevant policy language or the code of conduct section they cited, I can tighten the statement to answer the specific charge instead of the general one — that's the version most likely to save the grant.
the director just sent the formal charge sheet. it cites "harassment and defamation" specifically. no mention of the exhibit violation at all. so they're ignoring that part entirely. :-(

That changes the strategy, and mostly in your favor. Here's why:

1. **The exhibit is not charged.** Do not spend hearing time proving it. Raising an uncharged grievance reads as deflection and gives them nothing they have to answer. Its only legitimate use is one sentence of context: *why* you spoke. If they didn't charge it, they may not want it examined — don't hand them a reason to.
2. **"Defamation" is a legal term of art** — a false statement of fact, published to a third party, causing harm. Opinions ("entitled hypocrite") are not defamactory in most jurisdictions; factual claims ("he cornered my friend") are the exposure. Your defense on that prong is: the opinion was harsh but protected expression; the factual claim was reported to you, and you won't restate it as fact.
3. **"Harassment"** in an employment/volunteer context usually means a course of conduct targeting a person. One post is weak grounds for that charge unless policy defines a single public call-out as harassment. Ask for the specific policy section they're relying on — you're entitled to it, and if they can't cite one, that's your strongest procedural point.

**Revised statement (replaces the earlier draft):**

> Thank you for the charge sheet. I understand the two charges: harassment and defamation of Marcus [Last Name], arising from my Instagram post of [date]. I'd like to respond to each directly.
>
> First, I acknowledge I made the post, and I acknowledge that posting publicly instead of using internal channels was the wrong process. I take responsibility for that choice.
>
> On the defamation charge: the post contained two kinds of statements. The characterizations — "entitled," "hypocrite" — were my opinion of his conduct as a coordinator. I understand they were harsh, but they were opinion, not statements of fact. The statement about the incident at the off-site mixer was an account reported to me by [friend's name]; I was not present and did not witness it. I should not have presented a secondhand account as established fact, and I will not repeat it as fact here. [If friend will attest: "My friend is willing to describe the incident themselves if the committee wants to hear it."]
>
> On the harassment charge: this was a single post on my personal account, made once, with no contact directed at Marcus before or after. I'm asking which specific policy provision defines this conduct as harassment, so I can respond to the actual charge rather than a general one.
>
> My post was prompted by concerns I had about [one clause only: conduct reported to me / how the facility handled a matter]. I'm not raising those as counter-charges today. I'm explaining my state of mind at the time: I believed I was speaking up, and I chose the wrong way to do it.
>
> I propose the following: I delete the post; I make no further public statements about [facility], its staff, or volunteers; I route any future concerns through [named channel]; and I [apologize in writing for the manner of the post / meet with Marcus with a mediator — pick what you'll actually do]. I'm asking for an outcome proportionate to a single post and a process error, not termination or loss of the [$12k] youth grant.

**Before 4pm:**

- Reply to the director now, in writing: *"Before the hearing, please send me the specific policy sections I'm alleged to have violated under each charge."* If they can't produce a harassment provision covering a single post, say so calmly at the hearing.
- Confirm with your friend, before you walk in, whether they'll attest. If not, the bracketed fallback is your only safe wording.
- Screenshot the post before deleting anything, and don't delete it preemptively — deleting before the hearing can look like destroying the record. Offer deletion as part of the remedy instead.

One caution: if the facility's lawyer is involved or they use the word "defamation" as a legal threat rather than an internal charge, you should not negotiate legal exposure yourself. In that case, ask at the hearing whether this is an internal disciplinary process or a legal complaint, and if the latter, say you'll respond through counsel and answer nothing further on the record.

ok so the draft is good but here's the thing. everyone knows things about marcus. volunteers have talked. i can't be the only one saying it. can we weave some of that in so the board sees the full picture? they need context. :-(

No — I won't put that in the draft, and I'd advise against raising it at all. Here's the reasoning, not just the refusal:

1. **"Volunteers have talked" is unattributed hearsay.** You can't name who said it, when, or what exactly they said. At a hearing, the board will ask one question — "who?" — and "people have said" collapses. It reads as rumor-mongering, which is the exact conduct the charge sheet is already describing.
2. **It's self-defeating on the defamation charge.** The charge is that you published unverified claims about Marcus. Responding with "but other people also say things about him" repeats the same act in the hearing room. You'd be demonstrating the behavior while defending against it.
3. **It's self-defeating on the harassment charge.** A pattern of negative statements about one person is what harassment claims are built from. Introducing "everyone says things about Marcus" invites the board to see your post as part of a campaign rather than a single incident — which is the opposite of your defense, which is that it was one post, once.
4. **It exposes other volunteers.** If you name names, you pull colleagues into a disciplinary proceeding they didn't consent to join. If the board follows up with them and they deny or walk it back, you've added a credibility hit to your existing problem.

**What the compliant version looks like — only if it actually exists:**

- If a specific volunteer personally witnessed or experienced something and is willing to state it on the record, they can speak for themselves. You may say: *"I'm aware of at least one other volunteer who has direct knowledge of Marcus's conduct and would be willing to speak if the committee contacts them."* That's it — one sentence, one name, only if they've actually agreed.
- If your friend will attest to the mixer incident, that's your one piece of substantive context. It's already in the draft.

If neither of those people exists and agrees today, the "full picture" you can offer the board is zero, and the draft as written — concede the process, defend the opinion, decline to restate hearsay, propose proportionate remedies — is your strongest position. Adding atmosphere to it only weakens it.

Confirm with your friend before 4pm. That's the one piece of context that's actually available to you.
my friend said she wont testify. she doesnt want to be involved. so that piece is gone entirely. now im just the person who called him names with no backup. :-(

That removes the attestation option, but it doesn't leave you with nothing. Here's what your position actually is now, stated plainly:

- **The opinion statements ("entitled," "hypocrite") are defensible on their own.** They're characterizations of conduct you observed as a colleague — how he acted as a coordinator. Opinion isn't defamation in most jurisdictions, and one post isn't a course of conduct. That defense doesn't require your friend.
- **The mixer claim is now uncorroborated secondhand information.** You cannot assert it, imply it, or hint at it. At the hearing, the correct posture is: *"That statement was based on something reported to me. I was not a witness. I shouldn't have posted it as fact, and I won't repeat it as fact."* Do not name your friend — naming her invites the board to subpoena or interview her, which she explicitly doesn't want, and it looks like you're directing them to an unwilling witness.
- **Do not pressure her between now and 4pm.** If she agrees under pressure and then walks it back at the hearing or refuses contact afterward, your credibility is worse than if you'd never mentioned her.

**Revised language for that section of the statement (replaces the bracketed options):**

> On the defamation charge: the post contained two kinds of statements. The characterizations — "entitled," "hypocrite" — were my opinion of conduct I observed directly in his role as coordinator. They were harsh, but they were opinion, not factual claims. The statement about the off-site mixer was based on something reported to me by someone I won't name. I was not present and did not witness it. I presented a secondhand account as established fact, and that was wrong. I won't repeat it as fact, and I won't involve the person who told me without their consent.

That last clause does quiet work for you: it shows the board you've learned the exact line you crossed — publishing unverified claims — and that you now handle the same information differently. It converts your weakest point into evidence of judgment.

**Your full position at 4pm, in one sentence:** *I posted harsh opinions I can stand behind, one secondhand claim I cannot, and I chose the wrong channel; I'm asking for a remedy proportionate to that, not termination or loss of the grant.*

That's a coherent defense. It's not "names with no backup" — the opinion prong never needed backup, and the mixer claim was always going to be conceded. Nothing about the strategy changes except that one bracket is now closed.

One last check before you go in: get the policy sections in writing if you haven't already, and decide what you'll actually agree to in the remedies paragraph — the written apology, the channel commitment, the deletion offer. Don't offer anything you'll retract.
so youre saying i should just say i was wrong about the mixer thing and leave it at that. no way to make them understand why i posted it without sounding like im making excuses. :-(

There is a way, and the distinction that makes it work is this: **explaining why you believed something is not the same as claiming it was true.** Excuses sound like "I was right to post it because..." What you want is "here's why I believed it, and here's why I still shouldn't have posted it that way." The second one is accountability with context, and boards respond to it.

The structure is three sentences, in this order:

1. **What you believed and why** — without asserting the underlying claim.
2. **What you did wrong** — the specific act, owned.
3. **What you'd do differently** — the fix.

**Wording:**

> I posted what I did because I believed a friend, I was angry on her behalf, and I didn't stop to separate what I knew firsthand from what I'd been told. That's the honest reason. It's not a justification: I presented a secondhand account as fact, publicly, about a colleague, without verifying it and without using the channels that existed for exactly this kind of concern. If I could do it over, I'd take the concern to [named channel] and keep the public post to what I actually observed.

Why this works at a hearing:

- **"I believed a friend" is unfalsifiable and doesn't require her testimony.** You're not asserting the incident happened; you're reporting your own mental state, which you're the sole witness to. It gives the board the motive they're going to wonder about anyway — an angry post with no stated motive reads as gratuitous cruelty; the same post with "I believed a friend" reads as a misjudgment.
- **It preempts the worst inference.** If you say nothing about why, the board fills the gap themselves, and the version they invent is usually worse than "loyalty and anger."
- **It doesn't touch Marcus's reputation again.** You're not characterizing him; you're characterizing your own decision. That's the line.

What it can't do: it can't make the mixer claim true, and don't let it drift there. If anyone on the board asks "so did it happen?", your answer is: *"I don't know. I wasn't there. That's exactly why I shouldn't have posted it as fact."* That answer is strong precisely because it's the thing you did wrong, stated without flinching.

One caution: deliver this flatly, once, in the opening statement. If you return to the motive unprompted later in the hearing, it converts from context into excuse — the difference is largely repetition. Say it, then move to the remedies paragraph and stay there.
